title: Don't follow what you don't know
hook: hearing, sight and heart will all be asked about (17:36)

segments.voice: Yesterday: not tight-fisted, and not wasteful. Your line was the middle hand.

A screenshot arrives in the family group chat. It looks official. It says something shocking about a celebrity, or a medicine, or a neighbor's shop. Your thumb is already on the forward button. It takes one second to pass it on, and nobody will ever check who started it. Surah seventeen has a verse for that second. It's short, and it ends with three things you carry everywhere.

Verse thirty-six begins, in Pickthall's words: "follow not that whereof thou hast no knowledge." The Arabic verb is la taqfu, from qafa, the back of the neck. To follow, in this word, is to walk behind something, eyes on its back, going wherever it goes, without ever stepping around to see its face. Then the verse names three witnesses: the hearing, the sight, and the heart. Each one, it says, will be asked about. Not just the tongue that repeats something, but the ear that took it in, the eyes that read it, and the heart, the fu'ad, that decided to believe it. Al-Hujurat says it from another side: if someone of doubtful character brings you news, verify it, fa-tabayyanu, make it clear, so you don't harm people out of ignorance and end up regretting it. And Imam Muslim, at the opening of his hadith collection, reports a saying of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: it's enough of a lie for a person to pass on everything they hear. Not to invent. Just to pass on. That's the striking part: the warning isn't only against making things up, but against carrying things you haven't checked. The hadith scholars' habit of checking chains of narrators before accepting a report shows the same concern. The verse asks the same of a group chat.
screen: `LA TAQFU: WALKING BEHIND IT.` · `HEARING, SIGHT AND HEART.` · `VERIFY: MAKE IT CLEAR.` · `ENOUGH OF A LIE TO PASS IT ALL ON.` · then, large: `FOLLOW NOT THAT WHEREOF THOU HAST NO KNOWLEDGE.`

segments.voice: Let your attention rest on your ears for a few breaths, then on your eyes, then on your chest, where people often feel the heart: three gates. Now think of one thing you heard or read this week and passed on, or believed, without checking. Don't scold yourself; just ask, do I actually know this?
Fu'ad. The heart named among the witnesses in 17:36: hearing, sight and the fu'ad, each held responsible for what it takes in. Today's word.
Your line: you'll be asked about it. The ear, the eye and the heart all count. That's day four hundred sixty.

howItsDone: Muslim scholars cite 17:36 and 49:6 as the basis for verifying reports before acting on them or passing them on, the same concern that shaped the science of checking hadith narrators; preachers today often apply it to social media.
